interpretations.rationale:
Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted without any refusal keyed to its suffrage and does not install that member as leader; the attempt instead forces an election round in which every member's term advances, leadership lands on a member the caller did not name, and leadership is absent for a measurable interval in the earlier five-member receipts, while the four-member receipt below recorded no leaderless sample. Evidence, five receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Parsed index 3 of both receipts, the trigger where one non-leader member was demoted with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with an empty future_error, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. A successor run, receipt 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d, corrects the earlier measurement: the target's own configuration is read after DemoteVoter returns and polled until it changes (demotion_converged=true, demotion_converge_ms=0), and at the moment the transfer is requested the target itself reports target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter, so the member's own view already showed it held no vote; it still campaigned (7 candidate samples, 7 leaderless samples, target_term_after=4, target_ever_leader=false, future_ok=true with an empty error) while the voter control at parsed index 1 installed the named target and produced 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples. In receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f the trigger produced 8 candidate samples with 8 leaderless samples (about 80 ms with no member reporting Leader) out of 470 samples at roughly 10 ms spacing, against 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471 in that run's control. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and all other members at 4, one step beyond the rejected round) and its leaderless interval match exactly that path, while the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Clean-copy repeat, receipt 3324fe87d6da49c6b53eab0e116823df (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): re-executing the corrected experiment from its retained inputs reproduced the pair. Parsed index 0, the voter control: target_role_in_own_config=voter, future_ok=true in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, and 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471. Parsed index 2, the trigger case: target_demoted=true, demotion_converged=true at 0 ms and target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter; parsed index 3: future_ok=true with an empty error in 2 ms, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, 6 candidate samples and 6 leaderless samples (about 60 ms) out of 470, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4. The corrected result is therefore observed twice with the target's own configuration confirming the non-voter role at request time. Demotion race, receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d (twenty attempts, each on a fresh four-voter cluster): the harness started DemoteVoter for a follower and immediately issued LeadershipTransferToServer for the same member, without waiting for the demotion to commit or for any voter to apply it. Parsed index 1 records demote_ok_count=20, transfer_ok_count=20, target_led_count=0, final_target_count=0 and target_ended_nonvoter=20, with no transfer error. Issuing the two requests back to back therefore cannot install a member whose vote is being removed: the transfer is admitted and reports success, and the election it provokes is still rejected because the voters' applied configuration decides the outcome. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member receives a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, an extra election round that raises every member's term, and a leaderless interval whose length follows the configured election timeout.

Entry-point comparison, receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): one four-member cluster per case, one follower demoted in each, and the demoted member's own configuration view reporting the non-voter role before the transfer, converging in 0 ms in the control and 6 ms in the trigger. Parsed index 0 records the control's state and parsed index 1 its result: the automatic LeadershipTransfer() needed one attempt, its future returned nil in 106 ms, leadership ended on a voter that is not the demoted member, no leaderless sample was seen in 26 samples over three seconds, and a client Apply and a GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. Parsed index 2 records the trigger's state and parsed index 3 its result: five attempts spanning 1035 ms each returned 'leadership transfer in progress', the named member never reported Leader across the same 26 samples, the final leader is a different voter, and the client Apply and GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded. The control therefore shows that transfer works on this cluster shape and that the automatic path avoids the demoted member, while the explicit path admits the named member, keeps reporting a transfer in progress, and never installs it; both the earlier nil futures and this receipt's in-progress errors are consistent with the same gap, since neither is a refusal keyed to the target's lack of a vote.

Transfer-state probe, receipt 78769a572c5b4b249e441ac7ce63422a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same demote-then-transfer setup run twice with the leader's leadership-transfer flag sampled around each call. Parsed index 0 records the single-case state and parsed index 1 its result: the flag read false before the call, false as soon as the future was returned, false after the future completed and false three hundred milliseconds later; one attempt completed in 0 ms with no error, the named member never reported Leader across 283 samples over three seconds, no sample was leaderless, and the final leader is a different member. Parsed index 2 records the retry-case state and parsed index 3 its result: the flag read false before the first attempt, that attempt returned no error so the loop stopped after one, the named member never led across 284 samples, six samples were leaderless (about 60 ms), and the final leader is again a different member. Two things follow. The request was issued with no transfer already running and the library nevertheless accepted the demoted member as a target and reported the transfer as complete, so the earlier receipt's in-progress error is not evidence of a pre-existing transfer; and because the future succeeds while the named member never leads, the surface the caller sees is success, not a refusal, which is the form of the gap the account claims.

Repeat of the entry-point comparison, receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): the same fixed inputs were run again with no changes. Parsed index 0 records the control's state and parsed index 1 its result: one automatic attempt completed in 106 ms with no error, leadership ended on a voter that is not the demoted member, no leaderless sample was seen in 26 samples, and a client Apply and GetConfiguration afterwards both succeeded in about 2 ms. Parsed index 2 records the trigger's state and parsed index 3 its result: the first attempt already returned 'leadership transfer in progress', all five attempts over 1036 ms returned the same error, the named member never reported Leader, the final leader is a different voter, and the post-transfer Apply and GetConfiguration both succeeded. The in-progress surface therefore reproduces exactly in this harness across two runs, with the same error, the same five attempts and the same roughly one-second span, so it is a stable property of this sequence rather than a one-off event; the flag probe's clean first call remains a different sequence, and the difference between them is not yet identified.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.

The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general. The repeat reproduced that control as well, with the named voter installed and no leaderless samples.

The measured disruption is small in absolute terms because the cluster ran with inmemConfig timeouts (Heartbeat/Election/Lease 50 ms): the three trigger runs recorded 8, 7 and 6 leaderless samples (about 80, 70 and 60 ms) and one extra election round, against zero leaderless samples in the voter controls. The interval follows the configured election timeout, so a production configuration of about 1 s would scale it accordingly; these millisecond figures are not a bound for other settings.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.

Both corrected runs show the target's own configuration had already converged to non-voter before the request, so the exercised case is a member that knew it could not win; a demoted member whose own view still lagged (a stale configuration) was not exercised, although the earliest runs exercised an unknown mix.

The demotion race is a negative result for elevation: in 20 attempts issued back to back, no target became leader and every transfer reported success, so the timing gap that could have produced a worse outcome did not do so in this harness.

The future's result is not uniform across receipts: the demotion race receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d recorded successful transfer futures in all twenty attempts, while receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b recorded 'leadership transfer in progress' on every one of five attempts on a four-member cluster whose demoted member's view had already converged. The sentence that the future completes without error therefore describes those receipts and not the operation in general, and the durable observation common to both is that the named member is never installed and no suffrage check refuses it. The repeat of the entry-point comparison, receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586, reproduced the in-progress surface exactly, with the same error on all five attempts over 1036 ms, so within that harness the surface is stable.

The in-progress error seen in receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b is not reproduced here: with the transfer flag clear before the call, the same explicit request returned no error at all. The account therefore cannot claim that the error is a stable consequence of naming a non-voter, only that neither outcome is a refusal keyed to the target's suffrage and neither installs the target.
limitations: The cluster size is four members throughout, with three voters after the demotion, and the transfer always targets a non-leader member. The demotion race covers a transfer issued concurrently with the demotion, but a cluster whose only non-voter is the sole reachable member and a transfer that lands while the leader is already losing office to another election were not tested.

Leaderless counts are sampled every ~10 ms over roughly 4.7 s of the 5 s window (470 to 471 samples); a gap shorter than the sample spacing would be missed, so 60 to 80 ms is a lower bound for the trigger and the controls' zero does not prove uninterrupted leadership.

Only immediate convergence was observed in the corrected runs: the demoted member's own view reported the new role within the first poll (0 ms), so no single-case run exercised a target whose configuration still showed it as a voter at request time. The demotion race issues the transfer before applying, but it records the target's final role rather than its view at request time.
That the voter members had committed the demotion before the transfer is inferred from their rejection and term adoption, not from reading each voter's configuration.

Out of scope: whether an unprivileged or misconfigured peer could send TimeoutNow directly, even though timeoutNow performs no term, leader or membership check (raft.go:2232-2237); that path was not exercised here.

The in-progress surface is now shown to be stable inside the entry-point harness, which reproduced it on a second run, and absent in the flag-probe sequence, where the first call returned no error; the two harnesses differ in their preceding steps, including repeated leader and configuration polling before the transfer, and which of those steps sets the transfer state is not yet identified. Both measurements keep the demoted member's own view reporting the non-voter role before the call.
interpretations.joint_history: All five receipts belong to this investigation. Receipts d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba, 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f and 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d are successive revisions of the same fixed experiment: the first run, a revision adding per-member state sampling, and the revision that reads the target's own configuration after the demotion. Receipt 3324fe87d6da49c6b53eab0e116823df is a clean-copy repeat of the third revision executed from its retained inputs, with identical case names, admissions and assertions. Receipt 62e8b8bdcc9f448687b6588dda84125d comes from a separate experiment identifier, cf5136d55dd74f22ad66c73229d55f35-experiment, which keeps the same demote-then-transfer sequence but starts both requests back to back on a fresh cluster per attempt and summarises twenty attempts; it intervenes on the same mechanism under the same question, and its outcome is compatible with the single-case receipts. Receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b comes from a further experiment identifier, 6f0e1da8cb8048f5b28060a73243fa6b-experiment, which keeps the same demote-then-transfer shape and adds an automatic-transfer control on the same four-member cluster shape plus a client write after the transfer attempt. Receipt 78769a572c5b4b249e441ac7ce63422a comes from a further experiment identifier, 2690c8dadb9c4631b3fe90d9626cadb9-experiment, which keeps the demote-then-transfer setup and adds sampling of the leader's transfer flag around the call, so the earlier receipt's in-progress error can be attributed rather than assumed. Receipt e023eecf02c74f4db5bc8c5a16fd3586 is a repeat execution of 6f0e1da8cb8048f5b28060a73243fa6b-experiment from its retained inputs, so its cases, admissions and assertions match receipt a319426e86514f45b2053a7b3bd8050b.

result.summary: Recorded receipt 334d7a88f3b244548f316bcdb42b779e, the repeat of the demotion race from its retained inputs. The randomised loop behaved identically on its second run: twenty demotions succeeded, twenty transfer futures completed with an empty last error, the named member led in none of the attempts, no attempt ended with it leading, and it ended as a non-voter in all twenty. The account keeps its violated conclusion and asserted defect claim and now records that its nil-future surface is reproduced, so the same explicit request has two independently reproduced futures outcomes, the nil one in the demotion race and the 'leadership transfer in progress' one in the entry-point harness, plus a single clean call in the flag probe. The counterevidence entry about the non-uniform future result is extended with the second run, and the limitation is sharpened to name all three harnesses and the reproduced or single status of each, keeping the observation that the difference lies in their preceding steps, including repeated leader and configuration polling, with the step that sets the transfer state still unidentified. The joint history notes that this is a repeat of the same fixed experiment matching the earlier receipt's cases, admissions and assertions.

knowledge.statement: NetworkTransport's connection handler decodes an AppendEntries request and treats it as a heartbeat exactly when the term is non-zero, a leader address is present, PrevLogEntry and PrevLogTerm are both zero, there are no entries and LeaderCommitIndex is zero; for that shape it looks up the registered heartbeat handler under its lock and, if set, calls it directly on the connection-handler goroutine and skips the consumer channel, otherwise it enqueues the request for the main thread.
knowledge.conditions: NetworkTransport with NewRaft having registered processHeartbeat; incoming AppendEntries request matching the heartbeat field pattern.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader arms the verification with the leader's own vote by setting the future's vote count to one, sizes the quorum with quorumSize, which counts voters only, and then registers that future on every entry of leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication creates for every configured server including non-voters; a successful heartbeat or AppendEntries from any of those streams calls notifyAll(true), whose vote increments the count and completes the verification once it reaches the quorum. With three voters the quorum is two, so the leader plus one non-voter acknowledgement completes a verification that no second voter supported.
knowledge.conditions: Leader with at least one non-voter replication stream and fewer reachable voters than the voter quorum.

knowledge.statement: RecoverCluster refuses to run without existing state, restores the newest usable snapshot, then replays every log entry after the snapshot index, applying only LogCommand entries to the FSM and tracking the last index and term; it then writes a new snapshot carrying the caller-supplied configuration with configuration index 1 and deletes the entire log range. The recovered configuration is therefore the operator's parameter rather than anything derived from the log, and entries the node held without cluster-wide commitment become part of the recovered baseline.
knowledge.conditions: Operator-invoked catastrophic recovery with existing log, stable or snapshot state.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated. With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft does not complete a legal replay of already-committed log entries once the replay needs more than 128 FSM dispatch batches; the caller never receives the *Raft, so the node has no way to start, serve or shut down. This is a startup progress failure, not a decision-safety failure: no commit, vote or membership decision was observed to be wrong. Basis, from receipt d61420dbc49a4072937b040aac55a51c (status completed, outcome tests_passed, exit 0, all four selected subtests passed, changed_target_files empty). Parsed index 1 (control, seeded commit-tracking store, 8192 committed entries = exactly 128 batches) recorded returned=true in 5 ms. Parsed index 3 (control, retained state of a real single-node cluster that committed 8300 commands through the leader/commit/apply path, restarted with a snapshot at index 8302 at or above the staged commit index 8301, replay 0 batches) recorded returned=true in 0 ms. Parsed index 5 (seeded store, 8193 committed entries = 129 batches, one entry past the channel capacity) recorded returned=false after 5000 ms with exactly one newly blocked goroutine matching (*Raft).processLogs and one matching (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs. Parsed index 7 (the same real-cluster prefix without a snapshot, staged commit index 8300 = 130 batches) recorded returned=false after 5000 ms with the same two newly blocked goroutines. Mechanism from source: api.go:606 calls restoreFromCommittedLogs before any background goroutine exists; api.go:753 calls processLogs(commitIndex, nil); raft.go:1303-1313 sends each commitTuple batch into fsmMutateCh and selects only on that send and on r.shutdownCh; fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 (api.go:560); its only reader runFSM (fsm.go:241) is started at api.go:637 after NewRaft returns; api.go:1065 is the only closer of shutdownCh and is reachable only through a *Raft. After 128 successful sends the 129th send therefore has no producer and no possible closer, so the block is permanent rather than slow. Discrimination: the controls and triggers share the same code path and differ in replay length only, 8192 versus 8193 entries on the seeded store and snapshot versus no snapshot on the identical real prefix, so log volume, snapshot handling and the producing cluster are excluded as competing causes; the goroutine match localizes the block to processLogs invoked from restoreFromCommittedLogs. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a node restarting with the documented RestoreCommittedLogs option and with more than 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond its last snapshot hangs inside NewRaft indefinitely while reporting no error.

knowledge.assertion: NewRaft calls restoreFromCommittedLogs synchronously and processLogs flushes batches into fsmMutateCh while runFSM starts only after NewRaft returns.
The startup replay can enqueue at most 128 batches, so 8193 or more replayed entries beyond the last snapshot have no enabled progress path with DefaultConfig.

counterevidence: RestoreCommittedLogs is not part of DefaultConfig (config.go:329-341 leaves it false), and with the option disabled restoreFromCommittedLogs returns immediately (api.go:725-727), so default-configured nodes cannot reach the blocked path.

A snapshot at or near the commit index removes the replay entirely: parsed index 3 restarted the same 8300-commit real prefix with replay_batches=0 and returned NewRaft immediately, so snapshot cadence bounds exposure to this path.

The trigger observations are 5000 ms observation windows, not infinite runs; permanence is claimed from the source-level absence of any consumer before NewRaft returns and from shutdownCh having no closer outside Shutdown on the returned *Raft, not from the timeout alone.
No incorrect commit, applied entry, vote or membership decision was observed in any case; the evidence contradicts only startup progress.
limitations: The threshold is exactly 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond the last snapshot. MaxAppendEntries is configurable and validated up to 1024 (config.go:370-376) while the 128-slot fsmMutateCh capacity is not configurable, so other settings move the boundary (8193 entries with defaults) rather than remove it; no configuration was varied here.

Parsed indices 1 and 5 seed the commit-tracking store directly; only parsed indices 3 and 7 rest on a real leader/commit/apply prefix, and there the staged commit index (8300) lagged the last log index (8302) because the leader stages the pre-dispatch commit index.

The with-snapshot control eliminated the replay rather than shortening it, so real-prefix restarts whose replay is between 1 and 128 batches were not exercised; that recovery region is inferred from source, not measured.

fsm_applied_sampled is one sample at the end of each window and was 0 in every case, including the returning controls where runFSM had not yet applied anything, so it is not used as evidence of completion.

Out of scope here: whether the installSnapshot and restoreUserSnapshot sends to the same channel can block indefinitely on a running node, where runFSM is already active and would provide backpressure rather than a permanent block.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the committed configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted, completes its future without error, and does not install that member as leader; instead the attempt costs an extra election round in which the members' terms advance and leadership ends on a member the caller did not name. Evidence from receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba (completed, tests_passed, exit 0; both selected subtests passed). Parsed index 1, the control case where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, future_ms=2, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the transfer mechanism itself works and advances terms by exactly the election that installs the named target. Parsed index 3, the trigger case where the same cluster demoted the target with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with future_error empty, future_ms=0, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, the harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer then replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and every other member at 4, one step beyond the term the rejected non-voter campaign would have used) matches exactly that path, and the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member gets a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, and a forced election round that raises every voter's term and places leadership elsewhere.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.
The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.
limitations: The harness waits 200 ms after DemoteVoter and does not separately assert that the demoted member had received the committed configuration; the voters' rejection and the term pattern are consistent with a non-voter target, but the target's own view of its suffrage at TimeoutNow time was not sampled.

The leaderless interval could not be measured: the sampler produced 43 samples over the 5 s window (about one per 116 ms, not the nominal 10 ms), and no_leader_ms_sampled was 0 in both cases, which is not evidence that leadership was continuously available.

Only one cluster size (four voters) and one demotion position were exercised, and the leader always initiated the transfer to a non-leader member; transfer from a leader that later regains leadership, and clusters whose only non-voter is the sole contactable member, were not tested.

The observation window covered the future's completion and roughly half a second of subsequent leadership sampling; later re-elections that eventually return leadership to the original leader were not tracked, so the persistence of the effect beyond that window is not claimed.
Out of scope: whether an unprivileged peer could send TimeoutNow directly, even though timeoutNow performs no term, leader or membership check (raft.go:2232-2237); that path was not exercised here.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a separate goroutine, as the fast-path contract permits, can persist a term lower than the term the node had already adopted; once the term has regressed the node no longer rejects a stale leader's messages, so it truncates an entry it had already applied at the higher term and applies entries from the stale leader's history. Evidence from receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the term sequence: after_newer_term=4, after_stale_term=3, persisted_term=3, term_decreased=true, and the recorded sequence of persisted current-term writes is [1 1 2 4 3], so the node wrote 4 and then 3. Parsed index 3, the consequence: after the regression the stale term-3 leader's AppendEntries was accepted (stale_request_accepted=true), the log at index 4 became "stale4" while the FSM still holds "new4" there, index 5 was applied from the stale history as "stale5", and applied and commit indexes both reached 5 (applied_entry_replaced=true). Mechanism from source: Transport documents the heartbeat handler as a fast-path, NetworkTransport invokes it from its connection handler, and NewRaft registers r.processHeartbeat (transport.go:58-64, net_transport.go:298-305, api.go:626-632), so appendEntries can run off the main RPC queue; appendEntries tests a.Term above r.getCurrentTerm() and later calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term), which persists and stores the value without re-checking what it read (raft.go:1470-1490, 2164-2172), so an older term decided earlier can land later; the heartbeat request carries no entries, no previous-log term and no commit index (replication.go:388-397), so the regression is the term write itself, and the subsequent acceptance and truncation are performed by the same entry path that trusts the current term (raft.go:1526-1566). Why the comparisons matter: the first asserts Raft's requirement that a server never lowers its persisted term, the second that an entry already applied at a higher term is never replaced; both were contradicted by the same sequence. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a follower with a delayed term write can end at a term below one it already adopted and then accept and apply a stale leader's conflicting entries, leaving its log and FSM describing different histories.

knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: InmemTransport ignores SetHeartbeatHandler, and the harness therefore invoked r.processHeartbeat directly on a second goroutine rather than exercising a real transport's dispatch, so the transport framing, timeouts and connection lifecycle of NetworkTransport were not part of this observation.

The regression needs the older term write to complete after the newer one; the harness forced that order with a stable-store hook that holds one currentTerm value. Without such a delay the read-then-write pair normally completes in order, and the probe establishes reachability rather than a rate of occurrence.

The stale term-3 and newer term-4 requests were crafted AppendEntries whose leader commit indexes are asserted by the request, not produced by a quorum of live peers; only one real node ran. The claim is therefore about the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); the divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed elsewhere.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 currently exists only between the log and the FSM, and would surface on a restart replay.
limitations: Single follower, single sequence, one forced interleaving: no repetition, no timing sweep and no concurrent load, so nothing is claimed about how often or how easily this occurs in practice.

The two competing leaders were modelled by crafted requests over the real consumer path; the obsolete leader's partition, its continued heartbeating and the newer leader's quorum were not produced by real nodes.
Only the term and leader writes of the fast-path were exercised; whether other concurrent fast-path effects interact with snapshot installation or configuration updates was not tested.
The fix boundary is unexamined: a compare-and-set term update would close this particular interleaving, but no protective mechanism in the captured code was tested against it.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a goroutine other than the main RPC loop, as the fast-path contract permits, races the node's term update: when the stable-store write it performs takes long enough, the term it decided to persist can land after a higher term already persisted by the main thread, leaving the node below a term it had adopted. Once the term is below the current leader's term, the node stops rejecting an older leader's messages and replaces an entry it had already applied at the higher term with that leader's entry. Evidence. interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. Evidence, two receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a node restarting with the documented RestoreCommittedLogs option and with more than 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond its last snapshot hangs inside NewRaft indefinitely while reporting no error. The operational restart path was measured separately in receipt f032fc49841048c9877653db9f877b27: a three-voter cluster committed 8400 commands, one follower accumulated them and staged its own commit index at 8400 with last log index 8402, and only that follower was restarted. interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a goroutine other than the main RPC loop, as the fast-path contract permits, races the node's term update: when the stable-store write it performs takes long enough, the term it decided to persist can land after a higher term already persisted by the main thread, leaving the node below a term it had adopted. Once the term is below the current leader's term, the node stops rejecting an older leader's messages and replaces an entry it had already applied at the higher term with that leader's entry. Evidence. Consequence, receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b: parsed index 1 records after_newer_term=4, after_stale_term=3, persisted_term=3 and the write sequence [1 1 2 4 3] (term_decreased=true); parsed index 3 records the stale term-3 request being accepted (stale_request_accepted=true), the log at index 4 becoming "stale4" while the FSM still holds "new4", index 5 applied from the stale history as "stale5", and both applied and commit indexes at 5 (applied_entry_replaced=true). Frequency, receipt 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8: with no added store latency, 200 concurrent attempts produced inversion_count=0 (parsed index 1, comparison holds), while the same 200 attempts with a uniform 0-2 ms delay added to every current-term write produced inversion_count=90 (parsed index 3, comparison violated). The two cases differ only in that delay, so the inversion is a store-write-latency-sensitive race rather than an artifact of a forced order. Mechanism from source: Transport documents the heartbeat handler as a fast-path (transport.go:58-64); NetworkTransport classifies an AppendEntries as a heartbeat exactly when the term is non-zero, a leader address is present, both previous-log fields are zero, no entries are carried and LeaderCommitIndex is zero - the shape the leader's heartbeat request builds (net_transport.go:660-690, replication.go:388-397) - and for that shape calls the registered handler directly on the connection-handler goroutine, skipping the consumer channel (net_transport.go:718-736), with NewRaft registering r.processHeartbeat (api.go:626-632). appendEntries tests a.Term above r.getCurrentTerm(), then calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term), which writes the stable store and afterwards stores the same value atomically without re-checking (raft.go:1470-1490, 2164-2172); the gap between the store write and the atomic store is where a concurrent higher-term writer can be overtaken. The subsequent acceptance and truncation run on the entry path that trusts the current term (raft.go:1526-1566). Consequence under the exercised conditions: a follower whose stable-store term write is delayed can finish below an already adopted term and then accept and apply a stale leader's conflicting entries, leaving its log and FSM describing different histories. A clean-copy repeat of the same fixed experiment, receipt b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c, reproduced the pair: parsed index 1 shows inversion_count=0 for the 200 no-delay attempts and parsed index 3 shows inversion_count=97 for the 200 jittered attempts, against 0 and 90 in the first run. The two runs therefore agree that the inversion is absent or rare without added store latency and common with 0-2 ms of it, while the exact count varies between runs.

knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: In the retained frequency run the zero-latency case produced no inversion in 200 attempts, so the trigger is latency rather than concurrency alone; a rate below one in two hundred would not have been detected, and this run does not bound the zero-latency rate.

The stale term-3 and newer term-4 requests are crafted AppendEntries whose leader commit indexes are asserted by the request, not produced by a quorum of live peers; only one real node ran in either receipt. The claim therefore rests on the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed elsewhere.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 exists between the log and the FSM and would surface on a restart replay.

The probe delivered the heartbeat by calling the registered handler on a separate goroutine rather than through a live NetworkTransport, so framing, connection reuse, timeouts and the response path were not exercised, even though the classified request shape and the direct handler invocation match that transport's source.

The delayed store is a generic hook that sleeps before persisting; no disk-backed store implementation was measured, so nothing is claimed about how often a real stable store's write latency exceeds the interleaving window.
limitations: Two timing modes, 200 attempts each, repeated twice on one platform: the jittered case produced 90 and then 97 inversions, and the no-delay case produced none in either run. These counts are properties of this harness's delay distribution, not a field rate, and a rate below one in two hundred remains undetected for the no-delay case.

The two competing leaders were modelled by crafted requests over the real consumer path; the obsolete leader's partition, its continued heartbeating and the newer leader's quorum were not produced by real nodes, and repeated attempts reuse one node's log.
Only the term and leader writes of the fast-path were exercised; whether other concurrent fast-path effects interact with snapshot installation or configuration updates was not tested.
The fix boundary is unexamined: a compare-and-set term update would close this interleaving, but no protective mechanism in the captured code was tested against it.
interpretations.joint_history: Both receipts belong to this investigation and run the same follower-side setup on the same snapshot; they answer different parts of the question. Receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b forces one interleaving with a held term write and measures what happens afterwards, while receipt 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8 repeats the race 200 times per timing mode without a hook and measures only the inversion count. Neither receipt's events establish the other's claim, and together they support one account because the mechanism, node configuration and request shapes are identical. Receipt b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c is a repeat execution of the same fixed experiment with the same saved inputs, run in a clean copy; it adds reproducibility under the exercised delay distribution and does not introduce a different basis.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. VerifyLeader reports success although the leader can reach fewer voters than the voter quorum it sized, because acknowledgements arriving on non-voter replication streams are counted as support. Evidence from receipt 7a54f3754b0b423aaf1ba6c0365367c0 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the trigger: five members were bootstrapped, two were demoted to non-voters, and the leader's transport was disconnected in both directions from the two remaining voters, so voters_reachable=1 against quorum_voters=2 while nonvoters_reachable=2; VerifyLeader completed with verify_ok=true and an empty error, and the node was still Leader. Parsed index 3, the control on an identically built cluster with the non-voters also disconnected (nonvoters_reachable=0): the same call completed with verify_ok=false and the error 'leadership lost while committing log', the node by then a Follower. The two cases differ only in whether the non-voters could answer, so the successful verification in the trigger is attributable to non-voter acknowledgements rather than to voter support. Mechanism from source: verifyLeader sets quorumSize with quorumSize(), which counts only voters (raft.go:1087-1100), but registers the verify future on every entry of leaderState.replState (raft.go:966-990), and startStopReplication creates a replication state for every configured server including non-voters (raft.go:583-600); any successful heartbeat or AppendEntries response calls notifyAll(true) (replication.go:100-112), which increments the verify future's vote count (future.go:274-293) and completes it at the voter-sized quorum. The library already uses the correct supporter set one function away: checkLeaderLease iterates the latest configuration and counts only voters (raft.go:1037-1050), so the two paths disagree about who can establish leadership. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a client that calls VerifyLeader to protect a read (api.go:927-931) is told the leader still holds a voter quorum while it can reach none of the other voters, so the guard against serving stale reads after leadership loss does not hold in a cluster that contains non-voters.

knowledge.assertion: VerifyLeader sizes a voter quorum but registers the verification on every replication stream, including non-voters, whose acks increment its vote count.
checkLeaderLease counts only voters, unlike VerifyLeader.

counterevidence: The verification returned before the lease check stepped the leader down, so the false success is bounded by the leader lease interval rather than permanent; in the control that same step-down produced the error the trigger avoided.
VerifyLeader returning nil installed no leader and returned no data; the harm requires a client to rely on it as the guard the documentation describes, and this harness issued no reads.

Non-voter reachability does show the leader is alive and connected, so a deployment that used VerifyLeader only as a liveness probe would not be affected; the code sizes a voter quorum, which makes quorum the stated intent.
The partition was modelled by removing in-memory transport routing in both directions between the leader and the voters, not by dropping packets or crashing members.
limitations: One configuration shape was exercised: three voters and two non-voters, with the leader cut from both other voters. Other suffrage mixes, a single non-voter, or a non-voter whose heartbeat is the only one in flight were not tested.

The exposure window was not measured directly: the harness observed the verification completing immediately after the partition and the leader still in Leader state; how long a false success could persist before the lease check stepped the leader down is bounded by LeaderLeaseTimeout (one second here) but was not sampled.
No client reads were issued, so the end-to-end stale-read consequence is inferred from the documented purpose of VerifyLeader rather than observed.
The demotions completed before the partition, but each member's view of the new configuration was not read back before the transport was cut.

An attempt to observe the end-to-end stale read (majority commits a newer value while the partitioned leader verifies) did not succeed in construction: once the leader is cut from the voters it steps down at its next lease check, and forcing the majority side to campaign immediately still left the partitioned node a Follower by the time the new value had committed, so a positive verification concurrent with an already-stale FSM was not captured. interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted, completes its future without error, and does not install that member as leader; the attempt instead forces an election round in which every member's term advances, leadership lands on a member the caller did not name, and leadership is absent for a measurable interval. Evidence, three receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Parsed index 3 of both receipts, the trigger where one non-leader member was demoted with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with an empty future_error, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. A successor run, receipt 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d, corrects the earlier measurement: the target's own configuration is read after DemoteVoter returns and polled until it changes (demotion_converged=true, demotion_converge_ms=0), and at the moment the transfer is requested the target itself reports target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter, so the member knew it could not win; it still campaigned (7 candidate samples, 7 leaderless samples, target_term_after=4, target_ever_leader=false, future_ok=true with an empty error) while the voter control at parsed index 1 installed the named target and produced 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples. In receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f the trigger produced 8 candidate samples with 8 leaderless samples (about 80 ms with no member reporting Leader) out of 470 samples at roughly 10 ms spacing, against 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471 in that run's control. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and all other members at 4, one step beyond the rejected round) and its leaderless interval match exactly that path, while the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member receives a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, an extra election round that raises every member's term, and a leaderless interval whose length follows the configured election timeout.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.
The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general.

The measured disruption is small in absolute terms because the cluster ran with inmemConfig timeouts (Heartbeat/Election/Lease 50 ms): the two sampled runs recorded 8 and 7 leaderless samples (about 80 ms and 70 ms) and one extra election round, against zero leaderless samples in the voter controls. The interval follows the configured election timeout, so a production configuration of about 1 s would scale it accordingly; these millisecond figures are not a bound for other settings.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.

The corrected run shows the target's own configuration had already converged to non-voter before the request, so the exercised case is a member that knew it could not win; a demoted member whose own view still lagged (a stale configuration) was not exercised in this receipt, although the earlier runs exercised an unknown mix.
limitations: Both runs exercised one cluster size (four members, three voters after the demotion) and one relationship: a leader transferring to a non-leader member. Transfer initiated while the leader later regains leadership, and clusters whose only non-voter is the sole reachable member, were not tested.

Leaderless counts are sampled every ~10 ms over roughly 4.7 s of the 5 s window (470 samples); a gap shorter than the sample spacing would be missed, so 80 ms is a lower bound for the trigger and the control's zero does not prove uninterrupted leadership.

Only immediate convergence was observed: the demoted member's own view reported the new role within the first poll (0 ms), so no case exercised a target whose configuration still showed it as a voter at request time.
That the voter members had committed the demotion before the transfer is inferred from their rejection and term adoption, not from reading each voter's configuration.

Out of scope: whether an unprivileged or misconfigured peer could send TimeoutNow directly, even though timeoutNow performs no term, leader or membership check (raft.go:2232-2237); that path was not exercised here.
interpretations.joint_history: All three receipts belong to this investigation and were produced by successive revisions of the same fixed experiment under the same snapshot. interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A configuration change whose log write fails is reported to the caller as failed, but the new configuration is nevertheless installed in the leader's in-memory latest configuration at the index the entry would have occupied. The node then treats that unstored configuration as authoritative: it re-elects itself with the shrunken voter set and reports a client command committed with only its own acknowledgement, while the other member of the committed configuration does not have that entry. Evidence from receipt 0e6dd623c01e43a4b9e33cafc544ecf2 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 0, the case event: two voters were bootstrapped, the leader's store failed exactly the configuration write, and afterwards latest_index_after_fail=3 with last_log_index_after_fail=2, while phantom_servers records the shrunken configuration containing only the leader itself. Parsed index 1, the result: remove_failed=true with remove_error 'injected store failure', latest_index_exceeds_log=true, re_elected=true, apply_ok=true, commit_index=4, leader_last_index=4 and peer_last_index=2, so commit_without_peer=true. Under the committed two-voter configuration a quorum is both members, so the command the client was told had committed at index 4 never reached a quorum of that configuration. Mechanism from source: appendConfigurationEntry dispatches the configuration entry and then, unconditionally, calls setLatestConfiguration with the new configuration at the dispatched index, reconfigures the commitment map and restarts replication (raft.go:1204-1244), while dispatchLogs' store-error path only answers the futures with the error and moves the node to follower (raft.go:1245-1296). quorumSize, electSelf and setupLeaderState all read that latest configuration (raft.go:1087-1100, 1999-2071, 456-468), so the phantom configuration governs both the election the node wins alone and the quorum it uses to commit. Consequence under the exercised conditions: after a transient failure to store a configuration change, the leader can adopt a voter set that the rest of the cluster never accepted and serve client commits that no quorum of the committed configuration holds.

knowledge.assertion: appendConfigurationEntry installs the new configuration in memory regardless of whether its log entry was stored.
quorumSize, electSelf and setupLeaderState derive voter sets from the latest configuration.

counterevidence: The phantom configuration exists only in memory: a restart rebuilds configurations from the log, so the effect is bounded by the node's uptime unless a later successful configuration write extends it, and the harness did not restart the node.

The commit without a peer required the store to fail once and then succeed: the harness fails a single StoreLogs call, and a persistent write failure would also block the later client command, so the exercised trigger is a transient store error rather than a permanent one.

The other voter never accepted the phantom configuration and still holds the committed two-voter view, so its own elections fail while the phantom leader lives; the harness observed the leader's side only and did not measure how long the peer stays unable to win.
No data was corrupted: the client command was applied to the phantom leader's own state machine, and the failure mode is a commit reported without a quorum of the committed configuration.
limitations: One configuration shape (two voters), one injected failure and one run; no repetition, no three-member cluster and no non-voter in the configuration.
The harness applies its command immediately after the node returns to Leader and does not test whether a later successful configuration change repairs or compounds the phantom view.
Restart behaviour, which is where the log-derived configuration would replace the phantom one, was not exercised, so nothing is claimed about recovery from this state.
The client-visible completion point was the Apply future returning nil; no read path through the FSM was exercised.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated. With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft does not complete a legal replay of already-committed log entries once the replay needs more than 128 FSM dispatch batches; the caller never receives the *Raft, so the node has no way to start, serve or shut down. This is a startup progress failure, not a decision-safety failure: no commit, vote or membership decision was observed to be wrong. Evidence. Receipt d61420dbc49a4072937b040aac55a51c (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): parsed index 1, seeded commit-tracking store with 8192 committed entries = exactly 128 batches at MaxAppendEntries=64, returned=true in 5 ms; parsed index 3, the retained state of a real single-node cluster that committed 8300 commands through the leader/commit/apply path and then snapshotted at index 8302 above the staged commit index, replay 0 batches, returned=true in 0 ms; parsed index 5, the same seeded store with 8193 entries = 129 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with one newly blocked (*Raft).processLogs goroutine and one newly blocked (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs goroutine; parsed index 7, the same real-cluster prefix without a snapshot, staged commit 8300 = 130 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with the same two newly blocked goroutines. Successor receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0) reproduced all four outcomes (parsed indices 1, 3, 7, 9) and added parsed index 5: the identical 8193-entry store state that hangs at MaxAppendEntries=64, replayed as 9 batches with MaxAppendEntries=1024, returned=true in 2 ms. That comparison holds entry count, log content, staged commit index and snapshot state fixed and varies only the batch size, so the stall is attributable to the number of batches relative to the 128-slot channel rather than to log volume, snapshot handling, store state or the producing cluster; the goroutine match in both hanging cases localizes the block to processLogs invoked from restoreFromCommittedLogs. Mechanism from source: api.go:606 calls restoreFromCommittedLogs before any background goroutine exists; api.go:753 calls processLogs(commitIndex, nil); raft.go:1303-1313 sends each commitTuple batch into fsmMutateCh and selects only on that send and on r.shutdownCh; fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 (api.go:560); its only reader runFSM (fsm.go:241) is started at api.go:637 after NewRaft returns; api.go:1065 is the only closer of shutdownCh and is reachable only through a *Raft. After 128 successful sends the 129th send therefore has no producer and no possible closer, so the block is permanent rather than slow. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a node restarting with the documented RestoreCommittedLogs option and with more than 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond its last snapshot hangs inside NewRaft indefinitely while reporting no error. The operational restart path was measured separately in receipt f032fc49841048c9877653db9f877b27: a three-voter cluster committed 8400 commands, one follower accumulated them and staged its own commit index at 8400 with last log index 8402, and only that follower was restarted. With a snapshot taken on that follower at 8400 the replay was 0 batches and NewRaft returned in 0 ms (parsed index 1, comparison holds); without the snapshot the same follower needed 132 batches and NewRaft had not returned after 5000 ms (parsed index 3, comparison violated). The boundary therefore reproduces from the follower's own appendEntries-driven commit staging, not only from a feeding leader. The boundary was then checked at a second batch size: receipt f8b98d790cc14664af8af17775d3cc48 replays 131072 committed entries at MaxAppendEntries=1024, which is exactly 128 batches, and NewRaft returned in 45 ms (parsed index 7, comparison holds), while 131073 entries, one entry further and therefore 129 batches, did not return within 5000 ms (parsed index 9, comparison violated). The same capacity limit therefore governs a replay whose entry count is sixteen times larger, so the boundary follows the batch count rather than the default entry count.

knowledge.assertion: NewRaft calls restoreFromCommittedLogs synchronously and processLogs flushes batches into fsmMutateCh while runFSM starts only after NewRaft returns.
The startup replay can enqueue at most 128 batches, so with DefaultConfig 8193 or more replayed entries beyond the last snapshot have no enabled progress path.

counterevidence: RestoreCommittedLogs is not part of DefaultConfig (config.go:329-341 leaves it false), and with the option disabled restoreFromCommittedLogs returns immediately (api.go:725-727), so default-configured nodes cannot reach the blocked path.

A snapshot at or near the commit index removes the replay entirely: parsed index 3 in both receipts restarted the same 8300-commit real prefix with replay_batches=0 and returned NewRaft immediately, so snapshot cadence bounds exposure to this path.

A larger MaxAppendEntries moves the boundary: parsed index 5 of receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a completed the very state that hangs at the default batch size, so a deployment that raises MaxAppendEntries enough for 128*MaxAppendEntries to cover its snapshot lag does not encounter the block.

The trigger observations are 5000 ms observation windows, not infinite runs; permanence is claimed from the source-level absence of any consumer before NewRaft returns and from shutdownCh having no closer outside Shutdown on the returned *Raft, not from the timeout alone.
No incorrect commit, applied entry, vote or membership decision was observed in any case; the evidence contradicts only startup progress.
limitations: The boundary is 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond the last snapshot, and it was exercised at two batch sizes: at 64 the boundary is 8192 entries (8193 blocked, 8192 returned) and at 1024 it is 131072 entries (131073 blocked, 131072 returned). The 128-slot fsmMutateCh capacity is not configurable and no case varied it.

The seeded cases supply the commit-tracking store state directly. Three restarts rest on a real prefix: a single-node leader (staged commit 8300, last log 8302, because the leader stages the pre-dispatch commit index) and a three-voter cluster follower in both the snapshot and no-snapshot cases (staged commit 8400, last log 8402).

The with-snapshot control eliminated the replay rather than shortening it, so real-prefix restarts whose replay is between 1 and 128 batches were not exercised; that recovery region is bracketed only by the seeded 9-batch case and inferred from source for the real prefix.

fsm_applied_sampled is one sample at the end of each window and was 0 in every case, including the returning controls where runFSM had not yet applied anything, so it is not used as evidence of completion.

Out of scope here: whether the installSnapshot and restoreUserSnapshot sends to the same channel can block indefinitely on a running node, where runFSM is already active and would provide backpressure rather than a permanent block.
